docs.title: FontLab web design system
docs.text:
The demo and reference site of fly-january, the documentation theme for FontLab and Vexy sites built with ProperDocs and MaterialX. Every page here is rendered by the theme it describes.

  • Tokens: the palette, type roles, grid and sizes, drawn live from the --fly-* variables.
  • Configuration: every extra.fly and page key, with examples the build validates.
  • Assets: the CDN copy of the theme for pages outside MkDocs.
  • Chrome: FontLab, Vexy, no or custom global bars.
  • Field guide: design patterns and component specimens for FontLab web pages, with copyable Markdown and HTML.
  • Showcase and brand assets: product imagery, wordmarks and banners.

Writing rules live in the FontLab writing guide.

docs.title: FontLab brand and product assets
docs.text:
Download original wordmarks, banners, app icons and screenshots for FontLab products, partnerships and press coverage.

  • Company wordmarks: editable logo font, Illustrator sources, PDFs and PNGs in the supplied black, gray and white variants.
  • Product banners: four 728 × 90 campaign themes in PDF and PNG.
  • FontLab 8: app icons, hero and slide headers, screenshots and store copy.
  • TransType 4: app icons, screenshots and composed screenshot layouts.

Each pack lists every original file with format and size. Assets previously published by fontlabcom/fontlab-design-assets now live in this catalogue.

docs.title: Using the assets
docs.text:
These assets belong to Fontlab Ltd. Use them to represent FontLab products and partnerships. Keep the wordmark intact: no stretching or recolouring beyond the provided tints. Ask before adapting an asset to a missing format or size.

For usage questions or a missing asset, open an issue in the Marketing repository.

See the same content in Basecoat, daisyUI and MaterialX. Switch between light and dark with the theme picker, then copy the compiled HTML or Markdown source from each specimen.

  • Buttons show variants, sizes, icons and joined links.
  • Cards and surfaces group a title, description and action.
  • Fields pair text inputs, selects and textareas with labels and messages.
  • Choices and switches compare checkboxes, radios, toggles and sliders.
  • Tabs switch between equivalent views.
  • Alerts, admonitions and callouts give status or context.
  • Badges, tags and keys identify states and keyboard shortcuts.
  • Tables compare the same records.
  • Disclosure reveals optional detail.
  • Dialogs focus attention on a task.

docs.title: Align the decision criteria
docs.text:
A table is useful once the reader understands the alternatives. Keep its rows concrete and its language parallel. A missing feature and a feature that has not been checked are different states; write the distinction in the cell.

Question Conversion task Editing task What stays central? Preserve the existing typeface Develop the design or behaviour What do you inspect? Names, outlines, spacing, kerning, family grouping The parts of the font you changed What source do you retain? Original font files Editable project and reference files Where do you check suitability? Current converter documentation Current editor documentation

On a narrow screen, the table can scroll inside its own container. A card comparison is better when each alternative needs several paragraphs. Avoid making readers swipe repeatedly between a row label and its values.

docs.title: Start with what every option must do
docs.text: Before the differences, show the parity: the things a reader expects of any tool in the category, each with a checked yes and the version. Readers coming from another tool want to know nothing essential is missing before they read what is different. Name one frame per reader: other editors for people who use them, free tools or doing nothing for occasional users. A short “who should switch” block can follow, including who should not. When we publish a list of tools that includes our own, say it is ours and state the order's criterion.

docs.title: Compare other makers fairly
docs.text:
When the table names another company's product, the layout itself makes claims. A full cell for our product beside a sparse one for theirs tells the reader the other product does less, whether or not that is true.

  • Fill every cell from what that maker publishes, with the source and the date it was read. Where a maker publishes nothing, write “not stated on [page], read [date]” in the same type size as the facts.
  • Compare like with like. A time-limited full licence and a reduced edition go in separate rows, even when both are the cheapest option.
  • Put a currency note in any row that mixes currencies, not only in the introduction.
  • Use product names, not other makers' logos or interface screenshots. A screenshot of another application's output appears only where the claim is about that output, cropped to it, named and dated.
  • A short list of questions helps readers compare on their own terms: can the licence move to a new computer, on how many computers may it be installed, what will the next version cost, which formats does it open and export, does it make variable and colour fonts, can it be scripted, which writing systems does it support. Answer each for every tool on the page, dated and linked.
  • Recheck the table when a competitor changes a price or a version, not only before publishing; a date in small print does not keep an old figure true.
  • State when the other product is the better fit.

docs.title: The typeface survives the format
docs.text:
Font libraries contain more than outlines. Names, spacing, kerning and family structure carry decisions that designers made for the way the typeface would be used.

A format change puts those decisions under pressure. A studio may still need the typeface for an identity or a book, even when its current applications no longer accept the original files. Conversion begins with the question of what must survive the move.

What got lost in the handover was hand-tuned data. Years of careful kerning. Style links that lined up with how a designer actually used the family. Naming that matched the printed specimen.

The FontLab article TransType, the converter that outlived the format follows that problem from an old font library to a working typeface. It also separates format conversion from further editing: the next job may be extending a character set, adding OpenType features or working on the family in FontLab.

The conversion still needs inspection. Compare the names and family grouping, then examine spacing and kerning in representative text. Keep the original files so you can compare what changed.

Captions under product images are read more often than the body text. Write each one as a complete claim with the product name, so it still works for the reader who looks only at the pictures.

Three small blocks help near the end. A “what you receive” list names the files, licence and access the buyer gets. A licence row states whether the licence expires and what the next major version is expected to cost, or that the cost is not yet set. A “reviewed on” date under the facts tells readers and answer engines that someone checked them.

  • A paid landing page. One action and a minimal menu, the same facts and terms as the product page, and kept out of search results if it exists only for paid traffic.
  • A free guide. The guide itself, readable without a form; any form offers something extra, such as test files or update notices.

docs.title: Make vector artwork from an image
docs.text:
Vexy Lines transforms photos and images into scalable vector artwork. Choose a source with visible differences in tone so you can inspect how a fill responds.

  1. Bring a source image into Vexy Lines.

    The product accepts PNG, JPEG, TIFF, BMP, SVG and PDF sources. Start with one image so you can compare the source and the marks produced by the fill.

  2. Choose a fill.

    Linear fills create engraving-like lines. Wave fills bend the strokes. Halftone fills use dots. Try the same source with more than one fill before you commit to a composition.

  3. Compose with layers and masks.

    Stack fills or put them in groups. Use masks to control where a fill contributes to the image. Inspect both the overall composition and the places where two treatments meet.

  4. Export the artwork.

    SVG, PDF and EPS carry vector output. PNG and JPEG provide raster output for sharing. Choose the format for the next application that will use it.

docs.text:

  • Do masks end where you intended?
  • Does the exported file open in the destination application?

These are checks for this tutorial specimen. They do not describe automatic validation performed by Vexy Lines.

docs.title: Campaign stories
docs.text: A campaign page needs one subject and a visible next step. Show the work, explain what changes in it, then give the reader a route to the product or lesson. A campaign can be generous with images while keeping the reading path short and deliberate.

docs.title: Lead with the work
docs.text:
The Vexy Lines source page moves from an image to fills, then to layers and export. This composition keeps that progression while putting the interface beside the opening claim. The source's price and licence language is not copied here, because this catalogue does not maintain prices; the button therefore names where the terms are. A live campaign either carries one terms line beside its button (price, currency, licence type and platforms, from the same source as the product page) or, like this specimen, names the destination so the reader knows the terms are one click away. Readers who must ask for a price often do not.

Vexy Lines

The image, line treatment and editing controls share one workspace.

Adapted from www.vexy.art/src_docs/md/lines/index.md, especially its opening, “Paint with algorithms” and “Inside the studio” sections.

docs.title: Pixels become lines
docs.text:
Vexy Lines transforms photos and images into scalable vector artwork: engraving lines, waves, halftone dots and letters. You choose the fill and direct the composition with layers, groups and masks.

The app reads tone, edges and shapes, then draws with mathematically defined strokes. The source image gives you the subject; the fill changes how it is drawn.

See Vexy Lines price and licence

docs.title: Give the reader a sequence
docs.text: The next section answers how the work proceeds. Four short stages are enough for a campaign overview. Put exact tool settings in a linked tutorial, where the reader has room to follow them.

docs.title: 1. Bring a source
docs.text:
Start with a PNG, JPEG, TIFF, BMP, SVG or PDF. A photo, sketch or other image supplies the tone and structure that the fill will interpret.

Source images

docs.title: 2. Choose a fill
docs.text:
Linear, Wave, Circular and Halftone fills give the same source different rhythms. Choose the treatment that makes the subject readable.

Fill overview

docs.title: 3. Compose the layers
docs.text:
Stack fills, group them and paint masks. A mask lets one treatment appear where you need it while another carries a different part of the image.

Layers

docs.title: 4. Export the artwork
docs.text:
SVG, PDF and EPS preserve vector output. PNG and JPEG provide raster copies for the destinations that need them.

Exporting artwork

docs.title: Close with a useful handoff
docs.text:
The closing section should answer the question left by the demonstration. A reader who wants to understand masks needs a lesson; a reader assessing the app needs product information. Keep those destinations named separately.

Continue the composition

Layers and masks let you combine treatments without asking one fill to describe the whole image. Start with the mask lesson if you want to control where a treatment appears.

Read the layer guide View current product information

Both layouts use the guide's field-guide.css. The feature stacks text before image below 800px; the process grid keeps the four stages in source order.

docs.title: Measure the route and label partner work
docs.text: Give every link into a campaign its own key, such as a campaign parameter or a dedicated code, so the store's records show which route produced purchases. Judge the route by purchases, not by clicks. When a campaign page shows work by a customer, partner or creator, credit the maker, link the source, record the permission, and say plainly if the maker was paid or received a free licence.

docs.title: Product portfolios
docs.text: A portfolio helps readers recognise differences among works or tools. Give each entry a subject, an image when it supplies evidence, and a destination. Keep the descriptions comparable while allowing one entry enough room to explain a more complex process.

docs.title: A family of visual treatments
docs.text:
The Vexy Lines page introduces fills through their different drawing behaviours. This portfolio uses three source images at the same scale so you can compare their line structure. Captions name the treatment; the surrounding text explains where to continue reading.

Linear. Parallel marks build an engraving-like treatment. Read about Linear fill.

Wave. Curved lines carry the image through changes in rhythm. Read about Wave fill.

Circular. Concentric fields establish a different centre and flow. Read about Circular fill.

Source images and fill names come from www.vexy.art/src_docs/md/lines/index.md. Captions are adapted for this comparison. Keep the images' proportions; cropping every treatment to an arbitrary strip would hide the difference.

docs.title: Release notes
docs.text:
Release notes identify a version, explain what changed and give readers enough detail to use the change. Put the version and date beside the title. Keep a short overview separate from the exact behaviour of each feature.

The specimens below adapt the archived FontLab 8.4.0.8887 notes dated 27 June 2024. They demonstrate a release-page layout and do not describe the current FontLab release or a current upgrade offer.

docs.text: FontLab 8.4 adds tool-relevant context menus, more control over node rendering and improvements to work with components. The release also adds ways to use components in a Mask as visual references.

docs.title: Tool-relevant context menus
docs.text:
FontLab's Toolbox gives access to sub-tools and operations for the active tool. In FontLab 8.4, more tools also have context menus, so you can reach their operations where the pointer is, even when the toolbox is not visible.

  1. Activate a tool in the Toolbar.
  2. Right-click the Glyph window.
  3. Choose the operation from the tool's context menu.

For the Eraser, Brush and Guide tools, the context menu appears when you release the right mouse button. These tools also use right-dragging, so their menu timing differs from most tools.

docs.text:
Shape Meaning in the archived release notes Circle Smooth node: smooth connection between two curve segments Triangle Tangent node: smooth connection between a line and a curve Square Corner node: sharp connection between two segments Rhombus Handle, an off-curve point

The Glyph Window preferences let you adjust the rendering of nodes and handles. The shape and colour settings communicate different properties; keep the shape descriptions available when illustrating the colour settings.

docs.title: Compose with layers and masks
docs.text:
Stack fills to give different parts of the image different treatments. Group related layers and paint masks to control where each fill appears. The Vexy Lines source page describes one mask per layer and project files that you can reopen and refine.

docs.text: FontLab product pages are useful test material for this docs theme because they mix app icons, product screenshots, short proof copy, and purchase-oriented links. The theme should stay restrained enough for a manual, but it should not make product visuals feel like afterthoughts.

docs.title: Vexy vector imagery
docs.text:
Vexy Lines pushes the theme harder than the writing guide. The imagery is brighter, denser, and more kinetic; the docs chrome should hold it without turning into a dark marketing landing page.

The reading column stays narrow for comfort while an image can slip into the right margin beside the text, keeping the words and the picture in the same eye line instead of stacking them.

Full-bleed images run from the left edge of the text all the way to the right edge of the viewport, so a wide studio capture can breathe without being boxed into the measure. Everything else — headings, paragraphs, lists — holds a steady, readable line length.

docs.title: Publish with FontLab
docs.text:
Start with the thing you need to explain. Choose a paragraph for an idea, a list for a sequence, or a table for facts readers need to compare. Add a card, a tab or a control when the content needs that structure.

This field guide takes you from text to complete pages. Each specimen shows the result first, then the HTML extracted from that compiled result. Where Markdown can express the example, you can copy its source too.

docs.title: One decision, three treatments
docs.text:
All three links below lead to the same FontLab page. Their implementations use MaterialX, Basecoat and prefixed daisyUI, in that order. Use the treatment that fits the surrounding content. You do not need to choose a library for an entire page.

Explore FontLab Explore FontLab Explore FontLab

The .fltheme-components wrapper supplies the shared Basecoat and daisyUI styles. MaterialX classes keep their md- names. daisyUI component classes use du-, including modifiers such as du-btn-primary.

docs.title: Build the page in reading order
docs.text:
1. Choose a pattern for the reader's next decision.
  2. Copy and adapt the compiled HTML or authored Markdown.
  3. Check the theme and setup before you reuse a component elsewhere.
  4. Read Type and emphasis for the smallest useful building blocks.

The examples use FontLab and Vexy content so you can judge line length, labels, screenshots and reading order with real material. Product text is attributed beside the specimen. Sample values in forms and data displays describe only the demonstration.

docs.text: Choose the smallest structure that carries the distinction you need. A badge can identify a status. It cannot explain why an export failed. A tab can group alternatives. It should not hide the next required step.

docs.text: The reader needs to… Start with… Add structure when… Understand one idea Heading and paragraph A caption, note or example needs a separate place Follow a sequence Ordered list Each step includes a screenshot or a decision Go somewhere Descriptive link One route deserves button emphasis Compare choices Table Each choice needs an image or a substantial explanation Enter information Label and native field Validation, suggestions or grouping are necessary Inspect optional detail Disclosure Several independent topics need separate summaries Finish a consequential action Named button and confirmation The user must review the consequence before committing

docs.title: Read the boundary before copying
docs.text:
MaterialX renders authored documents. Basecoat and daisyUI provide component styles, and some Basecoat controls include runtime behaviour. None of these libraries sends your form to a server or decides whether a font is ready to release.

If the example needs application code, keep that dependency beside it. A working disclosure can be copied with its native HTML behaviour. A search panel needs a real search source before it can find your documents.

The copy guide explains which parts of a specimen travel with the HTML and which are supplied by the host page.

docs.title: Copy and adapt
docs.text: The HTML panel contains the markup extracted from the compiled specimen above it. Attribute lists have become attributes; Markdown links, emphasis and lists have become HTML. The build creates the panel after the page renderer runs.

docs.title: Copy a specimen
docs.text:
1. Click Copy HTML below the specimen.
  2. Paste into a page with the required styles and scripts.
  3. Replace the text, destinations and sample values.
  4. Rename IDs and their references if you repeat the specimen on one page.
  5. Check the result at a narrow width and with the keyboard.

If clipboard access is unavailable, the button selects the code and announces the fallback. Use your system Copy command. You can also select code directly without JavaScript.

docs.title: Markdown becomes the displayed HTML
docs.text:
The title attribute, two classes and ID below are all authored in one attribute list. The compiled panel shows what the installed Markdown renderer made of it.

Read the FontLab manual

Attribute lists attach to the preceding inline element. For a paragraph or a list, place the attribute list on its own line in the position documented for that block. See Python-Markdown attribute lists.

docs.title: Keep the context
docs.text:
Copied with the HTML Supplied by your page Element names, classes and attributes Shared theme CSS and MaterialX content styles Wrapper elements inside the specimen The page's .md-typeset content container IDs and ARIA references inside the specimen Unique IDs across the whole destination page Explicit inline handlers, if an example includes them Any named application handlers described by that example Compiled links and image URLs A valid base URL for relative links

The copy is the initial compiled state. It does not record changes you make in a field, an open dialog or the runtime's internal widget state. Basecoat markup inserted later is initialised by basecoat.js and follows the page's light or dark mode through the theme's fly.js (setup). MaterialX widgets may need MaterialX's own page initialization; copying their HTML into an unrelated site does not install that runtime.

docs.title: Use Markdown where it fits
docs.text:
Use Markdown for prose, lists, simple tables, notes and links with classes. Keep controls such as <input>, <select> and <dialog> as HTML. The Markdown panel can include HTML wrappers with markdown="1"; it is the source that actually produced the specimen, not a proposed approximation.

The source marker format and final extraction hook are documented in src_docs/hooks/compiled_examples.py. Markers enclose one independent specimen; nested, duplicated or incomplete markers fail the build.

docs.title: Theme and setup
docs.text: This site is built with ProperDocs and MaterialX on the fly-january theme, which also ships the component bundle the specimens use: Basecoat 1.0.2 and daisyUI 5.7.44 (du- prefix), both scoped to .fltheme-components, so one component area can mix them without sharing their button, card or input class names.

docs.title: MkDocs and ProperDocs sites
docs.text:
Install the theme in the environment that builds the site. Until its first release is on PyPI, install it from a checkout of fontlab-www-docstheme:

uv pip install fly-january              # once released
uv pip install -e ../fontlab-www-docstheme   # until then, from a checkout

Then turn it on in mkdocs.yml and load the component bundle from the theme's CDN tree. Replace <version> with the release on the assets page:

theme:
  name: fly-january
plugins:
  - fly
extra:
  fly:
    chrome: fontlab
extra_css:
  - https://fontlab.dev/fontlab-www-docstheme/fly/<version>/components.css
extra_javascript:
  - https://fontlab.dev/fontlab-www-docstheme/fly/<version>/basecoat.js

Every extra.fly key, the page front matter and the global bar choices are on the configuration and chrome pages. The theme provides the page shell, fonts, palette toggle and dark mode; it does not provide every Tailwind utility (extra.fly.utilities loads the prefixed set).

docs.title: Pages outside MkDocs
docs.text:
A Webflow page, landing page or other HTML loads the same files from https://fontlab.dev/fontlab-www-docstheme/fly/<version>/, each listed with its sha256 in manifest.json. fly-tokens.css gives the colours, type roles and grid as custom properties; the assets page shows how to use them with the component bundle.

Layout recipes in this guide name their FontLab CSS classes; copy those styles with a recipe when the target page does not already load them. This site's component-reference.css keeps closed Basecoat dialogs hidden and stops MaterialX disclosure styles from restyling component controls; copy it too when the target page uses MaterialX.

The previous bundle, fltheme26, stays published for the sites that still load it.

Component areas follow the page's palette: the theme's fly.js gives each .fltheme-components root the bundle's dark class when the page (or the nearest element with data-md-color-scheme) is dark, including areas inserted later. An isolated area can pin its mode with data-fltheme-mode. This changes component colours, not the surrounding article's typography.

Dark component area

Explicit light and dark modes set the component surface and ink independently of the surrounding page. Omit the attribute to inherit the host palette. The headings inherit the card's colour explicitly because the host also styles headings independently of body text.

docs.title: Preserve runtime ownership
docs.text:
Load basecoat.js once: it discovers widgets inside component areas, also those added later. Let the host page own theme choice and persistence; do not add a second global theme switcher inside a specimen. Native HTML controls keep their browser behaviour, while application actions still need your handlers.

The upstream contracts are Basecoat installation, daisyUI configuration and Markdown in HTML.

docs.text: Use bullets for peers and numbers for actions that must happen in order. Keep each step executable on its own. If a step needs a paragraph of explanation, put that explanation before or after the list.

docs.title: A short list of capabilities
docs.text:
Vexy Lines supports several stages of vector composition:

  • Bring in a source image, such as PNG, JPEG, SVG or PDF.
  • Choose a fill that responds to the image's tone and edges.
  • Compose the result with layers, groups and masks.
  • Export vectors as SVG, PDF or EPS.

Adapted from the How it works section of Vexy Lines.

docs.title: A procedure with visible stages

  1. Bring a source image into Vexy Lines.
  2. Choose a fill.
  3. Compose the artwork with layers and masks.
  4. Export the artwork as SVG or PDF.

The steps adapt the same Vexy source. They describe the sequence without inventing menu labels.

  3. Publish pending

docs.title: Complex List Mode

  2. Name the reader.

  3. Name the decision they need to make.

  4. Rest the draft. Return when you can notice what the prose actually says, rather than what you remember intending.

  5. Cut in descending order. Remove repeated paragraphs, then repeated sentences, then words that earn nothing.

docs.text:
Vexy Lines transforms photos and images into expressive, scalable SVG and PDF vector artwork: engraving lines, waves, halftone dots and letters.

You direct the composition with layers, fills and masks. Export vector artwork for scaling, or a raster image for a quick share.

Adapted from Vexy Lines, www.vexy.art/src_docs/md/lines/index.md. No price or licensing promise is part of this specimen.

docs.title: Use the tokens on any page
docs.text:
fly-tokens.css declares the palette, greys, type roles, sizes and grid as custom properties, light values on :root and dark values under [data-md-color-scheme="slate"]. The one rule it applies is the root size (html at 90% of the browser's font size, 99% from 100em, 108% from 125em), which makes 1rem half a body line; it styles nothing else:

<link rel="stylesheet" href="https://fontlab.dev/fontlab-www-docstheme/fly/0.4.0/fly-tokens.css">
<style>
  .note { color: var(--fly-ink); background: var(--fly-cobalt-tint);
          font: var(--fly-body-weight) var(--fly-size-sm) / var(--fly-line) var(--fly-body-family); }
  .note a { color: var(--fly-cobalt-deep); }
</style>

The default type roles use three Adobe Fonts kits. Load the families your page uses:

<link rel="stylesheet" href="https://use.typekit.net/xht3uat.css">
<link rel="stylesheet" href="https://use.typekit.net/cna4jfp.css">

docs.title: fly.css and the components outside MkDocs
docs.text:
fly.css is written for MaterialX's markup (.md-typeset, .md-sidebar, …) and sits on top of MaterialX's own stylesheets. A fly-january build also rescales MaterialX's rem lengths to the smaller root (the plugin's 20/14.4 post-build step), which a page loading MaterialX's CSS from elsewhere does not get. Outside a fly-january build, use fly-tokens.css with your own rules, and the components bundle for Basecoat and daisyUI markup inside an element with the class fltheme-components:

<link rel="stylesheet" href="https://fontlab.dev/fontlab-www-docstheme/fly/0.4.0/fly-tokens.css">
<link rel="stylesheet" href="https://fontlab.dev/fontlab-www-docstheme/fly/0.4.0/components.css">
<script defer src="https://fontlab.dev/fontlab-www-docstheme/fly/0.4.0/basecoat.js"></script>

<div class="fltheme-components">
  <button class="btn">Basecoat button</button>
  <button class="du-btn du-btn-primary">daisyUI button</button>
</div>

This site loads the components bundle the same way, from fly/latest/, for the field guide pages.

docs.title: FontLab
docs.text:
The default. Loads https://i.fontlab.com/menu/fontlab.js and renders <fontlab-menu> above the page and <fontlab-footer> below it. This site uses it.

mkdocs.yml
extra:
  fly:
    chrome: fontlab
    chrome_options:
      site-label: Design system
      search-from: docstheme

The menu gets mode="dark", site-label (default: site_name), site-url (site_url), mobile-menu="materialx" and mobile-search="materialx", then the chrome_options you set. site-url there takes an absolute http(s) URL or a root-relative path such as /docs/, for a label that links somewhere other than site_url. search-from names the site in searches sent to search.fontlab.com.

docs.title: Vexy
docs.text:
Loads https://i.vexy.art/menu/vexy.js and renders <vexy-menu> and <vexy-footer> with the same attributes.

mkdocs.yml
extra:
  fly:
    chrome: vexy
    chrome_options:
      site-label: Vexy Lines

docs.title: None
docs.text:
No company bars: MaterialX's own header (site name, search, palette toggle, drawer button) and footer. Use it for unofficial sites.

mkdocs.yml
extra:
  fly:
    chrome: none

docs.title: Custom
docs.text:
Any script that defines two custom elements. The theme loads the script (deferred) and renders the header element before the page and the footer element after it, with the menu attributes above. MaterialX's header stays, so search and the palette toggle keep working.

mkdocs.yml
extra:
  fly:
    chrome:
      script: https://example.com/acme-menu.js
      header: acme-menu
      footer: acme-footer
    chrome_options:
      site-label: Acme docs

script must be an https:// URL; header and footer must be custom element names (with a hyphen).

Invalid: custom chrome without a footer element
extra:
  fly:
    chrome:
      script: https://example.com/acme-menu.js
      header: acme-menu

docs.title: Body classes
docs.text: The plugin marks <body> with fly-chrome-fontlab, fly-chrome-vexy, fly-chrome-none or fly-chrome-custom. The theme hides MaterialX's header only under the FontLab and Vexy bars.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: A site turns the theme on with two entries in mkdocs.yml and configures it under extra.fly. The fly plugin validates that block when the build starts: an unknown key, an unknown hue or preset, or a malformed value stops the build with a message that names the key. Every YAML example on this page goes through the same validation in the theme's tests (tests/py/test_demo_site.py).

docs.title: Turn the theme on
docs.text:
mkdocs.yml
theme:
  name: fly-january
plugins:
  - fly

custom_dir stays available for site-specific templates. A template override named main.html replaces the theme's own and drops its stylesheets and scripts, so prefer a hook or a partial for additions.

docs.title: Local and remote assets
docs.text:
By default, fly-january serves its CSS and JavaScript from the built site with content hashes in their URLs. Set extra.fly.assets: remote or select theme.name: fly-january-remote with the same fly plugin. Using fly-january-remote with extra.fly.assets: local fails the build.

Remote pages load Fly styles and scripts from https://fontlab.dev/fontlab-www-docstheme/fly/latest/. After a release and browser cache refresh, deployed pages pick up CSS and JavaScript changes without a site rebuild. Template and plugin changes require upgrading the Python package and rebuilding. Both modes use the installed MaterialX styles and scripts locally. Building in remote mode requires no connection to the asset host.

By default, remote mode runs JavaScript from fontlab.dev without Subresource Integrity (SRI). Pinning assets_url to a versioned folder limits exposure to future releases.

To pin Fly assets to one release, set the base URL including its trailing slash.

mkdocs.yml
extra:
  fly:
    assets: remote
    assets_url: https://fontlab.dev/fontlab-www-docstheme/fly/0.4.0/

docs.title: Site keys: extra.fly
docs.text:
Key Default Value assets local (remote alias: remote) local or remote assets_url Fly CDN latest/ Remote asset directory URL ending in / chrome fontlab fontlab, vexy, none or {script, header, footer}; see chrome chrome_options none menu attributes: site-label, site-url (an absolute http(s) URL or a root-relative path; defaults to the site URL), mobile-menu, mobile-search, search-from, and sticky (true pins the bar to the top; default false) hue none (accent cobalt) the accent: cherry, tangerine, amber, lime, emerald, teal, sky, cobalt, indigo, violet, magenta, rose or gray fonts.sources the theme's three small kits (below) stylesheets loaded on every page: typekit:<kit>, google:<css2 family spec> or an https:// URL; setting it replaces the defaults, [] loads none fonts.roles theme defaults per-role overrides, {<role>: {<property>: <value>}}; see tokens h1 ink ink or accent: whether every page title takes the hue's text colour; a page whose hue comes from its own front matter or preset always does, unless it sets h1: ink links inherit inherit or accent: article links keep the text colour, or take the accent's text colour (contrast-safe in both schemes) presets none named {fonts, hue} bundles a page can pick margin_side left where margin figures sit: left or right utilities false true loads fly-utilities.css, every Tailwind utility with the tw: prefix (1.9 MB) debug false true adds a preset switcher (fly-debug.js) for trying looks in the browser

The default Typekit sources are xht3uat for Polymath Display (H1) and Polymath (H2 and lead), cna4jfp for Sole Serif Small (body), and wck5koo for Grtsk (H3–H6, navigation, tables, inline sans and buttons). Setting fonts.roles alone keeps the default sources. Setting fonts.sources replaces the list, so include a source for each web font the site uses. Set fonts.sources: [] to use the system fallbacks. The prototype's Quire Sans exists only in an all-families kit (gav0zux, 654 KB), which the theme never loads by default: add it to sources and set the h2 family to use it.

A complete site block:

mkdocs.yml
extra:
  fly:
    chrome: fontlab
    chrome_options:
      site-label: Design system
      site-url: https://design.example/
      mobile-menu: materialx
      mobile-search: materialx
      search-from: docstheme
      sticky: false
    hue: cobalt
    h1: ink
    links: inherit
    fonts:
      sources:
        - typekit:gav0zux
        - google:Outfit:wght@100..900
        - https://example.com/fonts.css
      roles:
        h1: {family: "'newsserif-huge-variable', serif", weight: 700}
        h2: {family: "'quire-sans', sans-serif", weight: 300, scale: 1.1}
        body: {family: "'Outfit', sans-serif", features: '"onum" 1'}
        strong: {weight: 600}
        em: {style: italic}
        sans: {family: "'Outfit', sans-serif", stretch: normal, variation: normal, adjust: 1}
    presets:
      fl9-color:
        fonts:
          sources: [google:Blaka+Ink]
          roles: {h1: {family: "'Blaka Ink'", weight: 400, scale: 1.1}}
        hue: magenta
      plain:
        hue: gray
    margin_side: right
    utilities: false
    debug: false

typekit:gav0zux loads https://use.typekit.net/gav0zux.css; google:Outfit:wght@100..900 loads https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=Outfit:wght@100..900&display=swap. Join several Google families into one stylesheet with &family=:

mkdocs.yml
extra:
  fly:
    fonts:
      sources:
        - google:Outfit:wght@100..900&family=REM:wght@100..900

Role properties: block roles (h1, h2, h3, h4, h5, h6, body, lead, nav, table, caption, code) take family, weight, stretch, features, variation, size, leading, tracking and scale; h1 and h2 also take measure (a length in ch, rem, em, px or %, or none); inline roles: em takes family, weight, adjust and style (normal or italic); strong and mono take family, weight and adjust; sans (the face of links, marks and h6) takes family, stretch, variation and adjust. Values are plain CSS: a value that could end its declaration (;, braces, <, a comment or an unbalanced quote) is rejected.

These blocks fail the build:

Invalid: unknown hue
extra:
  fly:
    hue: crimson
Invalid: unknown key
extra:
  fly:
    colour: cobalt
Invalid: font source without a scheme
extra:
  fly:
    fonts:
      sources: [fonts.example.com/a.css]
Invalid: role value that ends the declaration
extra:
  fly:
    fonts:
      roles:
        h1: {family: "serif; color: red"}

docs.title: Page keys: front matter
docs.text:
A page can change its look. Precedence: page fonts and hue over the page's preset over the site. Font sources accumulate (each loaded once); roles merge property by property. These examples assume the site block above.

Page front matter
fly:
  preset: fl9-color
Page front matter
fly:
  preset: plain
  hue: teal
  h1: ink
  fonts:
    sources: [typekit:abc1def]
    roles:
      h1: {weight: 300}
      body: {features: '"onum" 1'}

The legacy key subtheme is read as fly.preset and also adds subtheme-<name> to <body>:

Page front matter
subtheme: fl9-color

Other page keys the plugin reads:

Page front matter
classes:
  body: [wide-page]
  main: ref-main
  article: [specimen]
margin_side: left
hide: [toc]

classes adds classes to the first <body>, <main> and <article>; margin_side overrides extra.fly.margin_side (fly-margin-left or fly-margin-right on <body>); hide: [toc] removes the page's table of contents (fly-no-l2).

These page blocks fail the build:

Invalid page: unknown preset
fly:
  preset: newspaper
Invalid page: subtheme and preset disagree
subtheme: plain
fly:
  preset: fl9-color

docs.title: Tokens
docs.text: Every fly-january rule reads --fly-* custom properties. The swatches and specimens on this page are drawn from those variables as the browser resolves them, so they show the values this release ships. DESIGN-TOKENS.md records where each value came from; fly-tokens.css on the assets page carries the same tokens for pages outside MkDocs.

docs.title: Palette
docs.text:
Twelve hues, each with a lead colour and a soft (lighter), deep (darker) and tint (surface wash) variant, nine greys and the paper surfaces. Light values apply to the default scheme, dark values to the slate scheme. Both panels keep their scheme whichever the palette toggle selects for the rest of the page. The columns are --fly-<hue>, --fly-<hue>-soft, --fly-<hue>-deep and --fly-<hue>-tint; hover a swatch for its name.

Light navigation sheets are #f6f7f8. On mid-desktop screens, the exposed strip of site navigation uses --fly-paper-1-covered (#eff0f1) until the page navigation retracts. All directional shadows use a 2px blur and 3% black in both schemes.

docs.text:
Twelve block roles, each with nine variables: --fly-<role>-family, -weight, -stretch, -features, -variation, -size, -leading, -tracking and -scale. docs.title: Grid and sizes
docs.text:
1rem is half a body line, and every vertical length in flowing text is a whole number of rems. The prose scale has three base sizes. Table text and controls default to 90% of body size. Card and dialog titles use a component token based on the large prose size. Admonition and disclosure titles follow the body or margin-aside size.

Token Value At the 14.4px root Use --fly-half 1rem 14.4px half a line; the vertical step --fly-line 2rem 28.8px the body line --fly-size-xs 0.9722rem 14px captions, table heads, navigation, footers --fly-size-sm 1.25rem 18px body text --fly-size-md 1.625rem 23.4px lead paragraphs, blockquotes

xs Captions and navigation sit at the small size.

sm Body text uses the middle size. Table data uses 90% of the body size.

md Lead paragraphs use the large size.

The root is 90% of the browser's font size (14.4px by default), 99% from 100em and 108% from 125em, so wide screens scale the whole grid while 1rem stays half a line.
